<reason>PRO built the more durable structural case: the symmetry argument (monopsony as mirror-image of monopoly), the unrebutted statutory point that the Clayton Act does not exempt labor markets, and the reframe of the evidence gap as a "policy choice" rather than a law of nature. PRO's grocery-market-messiness analogy directly answered CON's core claim that labor markets are uniquely hard to define, and CON's Rebuttal 2 never circled back to neutralize it. The decisive turn came in the pressure-question exchange: CON's A1 answer conceded that "proven" means the same preponderance standard already used for price effects, and PRO's closing exploited this cleanly, arguing that once the standard is admitted to be identical, CON's remaining objection ("don't even ask the question routinely") is itself asking for less seriousness than price effects already receive at every filing. CON never fully rebutted this collapse in the closing, instead reasserting the "coin flip" metaphor that PRO had already repurposed against it. CON's strongest sustained point, the resource-mandate/evidentiary-asymmetry argument, was well-maintained and its "alternative fix" (noncompetes, portable licenses) went unrebutted because PRO's relevant rebuttal was clipped for length — a real execution cost. PRO's case also suffered two word-limit clippings, which cost it some content and reflects a discipline lapse. But on the core clash that mattered most by the end, PRO's answers were more responsive and its closing move was sharper, giving it a clear, if not overwhelming, edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The exchange over "what does 'proven' mean" — CON's A4.1 concession that the evidentiary standard is identical to price-effects review, followed by PRO's closing (B5.1) collapsing that concession into an admission that "as seriously" only demands routine screening — was the most decisive clash, and CON never fully recovered from it.</best_rebuttal>
